docs.title: Authentication token lifecycle
docs.body:
---
description: How access and refresh tokens are issued, rotated and revoked.
---


# Authentication token lifecycle

## Access tokens

Access tokens are signed JWTs with a lifetime of **15 minutes**. They carry the
account id, the scopes and a `jti`. The gateway validates the signature locally
against the JWKS it caches for one hour; it never calls the auth service on the
hot path.

When an access token is past its `exp`, the gateway answers `401` with the error
code `ERR_TOKEN_EXPIRED`. Clients must then use their refresh token; they must
not prompt the user.

## Refresh tokens

Refresh tokens live **30 days** and rotate on every use. Each refresh returns a
new pair and invalidates the old refresh token. Tokens that descend from the
same login form a *family*.

```http
POST /oauth/token
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=refresh_token&refresh_token=rt_9f2c...
```

## Reuse detection

If a refresh token that was already rotated is presented again, the whole family
is revoked and the user must log in again. This protects against a stolen token
being replayed. See D41 for the 10-second grace window that was added after
mobile clients raced two refreshes.

## Revocation

- Logging out revokes the family.
- Changing the password revokes every family for the account.
- Support can revoke a family from the admin console (`auth:revoke` scope).

## Error codes

| Code | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `ERR_TOKEN_EXPIRED` | access token past `exp` |
| `ERR_TOKEN_REVOKED` | family was revoked |
| `ERR_TOKEN_REUSED` | rotated refresh token presented again |

docs.title: Rate limiting policy
docs.body:
# Rate limiting policy

Every API key gets a token bucket of **600 requests per minute**, refilled
continuously. When the bucket is empty the API answers `429 Too Many Requests`
with a `Retry-After` header in seconds.

- Buckets are per key, not per IP.
- Burst capacity is 100 requests on top of the steady rate.
- Internal service accounts are exempt; they are throttled at the mesh instead.
- Partner integrations sit on a separate tier (see the ruling on task
  "Raise rate limit for partner integrations").

Limits are enforced in the gateway by the `ratelimit` filter, backed by Redis.

docs.title: Pagination conventions
docs.body:
# Pagination conventions

All list endpoints use **cursor pagination**. Offsets are not supported because
they skip or repeat rows when data changes between pages.

```json
{
  "data": [ ... ],
  "next_cursor": "eyJpZCI6MTIzNH0",
  "has_more": true
}
```

- `limit` defaults to 50 and is capped at 200.
- Cursors are opaque base64; clients must not parse them.
- A cursor is valid for 24 hours.

docs.title: Error envelope format
docs.body:
# Error envelope format

Every non-2xx response has the same JSON body:

```json
{ "error": { "code": "ERR_VALIDATION", "message": "email is required", "request_id": "req_81ab" } }
```

Codes are stable and documented; messages are for humans and may change.

Common codes: `ERR_VALIDATION` (422), `ERR_NOT_FOUND` (404), `ERR_TOKEN_EXPIRED`
(401), `ERR_FORBIDDEN` (403), `ERR_QUOTA_EXCEEDED` (429), `ERR_CONFLICT` (409),
`ERR_INTERNAL` (500). Always include `request_id` when filing a bug.

docs.title: API versioning
docs.body:
# API versioning

We version by date. Clients send `Api-Version: 2026-03-01`; a request without
the header gets the version pinned to the key when it was created.

Breaking changes only land in a new dated version. A version is supported for
**12 months** after its successor ships. Deprecated endpoints return a
`Deprecation` header and, once a date is fixed, a `Sunset` header.

Non-breaking additions (new fields, new endpoints, new optional parameters) ship
into every supported version.

docs.title: payments.rs module overview
Webhook delivery
docs.body:
# Webhook delivery

Events are delivered by POST to the merchant's endpoint. A delivery succeeds on
any 2xx within 10 seconds.

Failed deliveries retry with exponential backoff: 8 attempts over roughly 36
hours (1m, 5m, 30m, 2h, 5h, 10h, 12h, 6h). After the last attempt the endpoint
is disabled and the merchant gets an email.

Each request carries `X-Signature: t=<unix>,v1=<hex>`, an HMAC-SHA256 of
`t + "." + body` with the endpoint secret. Receivers should reject timestamps
older than five minutes to stop replays.

docs.title: Idempotency keys
docs.body:
Clients send `Idempotency-Key` on every POST that moves money. The server stores
the first response for 24 hours and replays it for any retry with the same key.
A retry with the same key but a different body gets `409 ERR_CONFLICT`.

docs.title: Client SDK support policy
docs.body:
# Client SDK support policy

We publish official SDKs for TypeScript, Python and Kotlin. Each major line gets
security fixes for 18 months after the next major ships. SDKs follow semver:
breaking changes only in a major. Generated code comes from the OpenAPI spec in
`api/openapi.yaml`; hand edits to generated files are overwritten.

docs.title: Search service
docs.body:
# Search service

Product search runs on a dedicated OpenSearch cluster fed by change-data-capture
from the catalog database. Indexing lag is normally under 5 seconds.

Queries go through `GET /v2/search`. Relevance tuning lives in
`search/boosts.yaml`; changes there need a before/after run of the relevance
suite (`make relevance`), which scores 400 judged queries.

docs.title: Frontend build pipeline
docs.body:
# Frontend build pipeline

The web app builds with Vite. `pnpm build` produces hashed assets in `dist/`
which CI uploads to the CDN bucket.

## Bundle budget

The main entry chunk must stay under **250 KB gzipped**. CI runs
`pnpm size-check` and fails the build over budget. Large dependencies (charts,
the rich-text editor) are loaded with dynamic `import()`.

## Source maps

Source maps are uploaded to the crash service and *not* served publicly.

docs.title: Design tokens and theming
docs.body:
# Design tokens and theming

Colours, spacing and type scales are design tokens in `tokens/*.json`, compiled
into CSS custom properties. Components never hard-code a hex value.

Dark mode swaps the token set under `[data-theme="dark"]` and follows the OS
setting unless the user picks one explicitly. New components must be checked in
both themes before review.

docs.title: Accessibility checklist
docs.body:
---
description: What every web change is checked against before merge.
---


# Accessibility checklist

We target WCAG 2.2 AA.

- Text contrast at least 4.5:1, large text 3:1.
- Every interactive element reachable by keyboard, with a visible focus ring.
- Images have `alt`; decorative ones have `alt=""`.
- Form fields have a programmatic label; errors are announced with `aria-live`.
- No motion that cannot be turned off; respect `prefers-reduced-motion`.
- Screen-reader smoke test with VoiceOver on the changed flow.

docs.title: Feature flags
docs.body:
# Feature flags

Flags are served by the internal Beacon service and read through
`useFlag("name")` on the web and `Flags.isOn("name")` on mobile.

Rules:
- Every flag has an owner and an expiry date.
- A flag that has been fully on for 90 days is removed; the cleanup bot opens a
  ticket.
- Flags gate code paths, not configuration values; config belongs in settings.

docs.title: Browser support matrix
docs.body:
We support the last two major versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari, plus
Safari on iOS 16 and newer. Internet Explorer is not supported. Polyfills are
added only through `browserslist`, never by hand.

docs.title: Checkout page performance
docs.body:
# Checkout page performance

Targets on a mid-range Android phone over 4G:

- Largest Contentful Paint under 2.5 s
- Interaction to Next Paint under 200 ms
- Cumulative Layout Shift under 0.1

The biggest win so far was server-rendering the order summary and deferring the
address autocomplete script until the field gets focus.

docs.title: Web internationalisation
docs.body:
# Web internationalisation

Strings live in `locales/<lang>.json` and are looked up with `t("key")`.
Supported languages: English, Dutch, German, French. Missing keys fall back to
English and are reported to the translation dashboard. Dates and money are
formatted with `Intl`, never by string concatenation.

docs.title: Mobile release train
docs.body:
# Mobile release train

iOS and Android ship every **two weeks** on Wednesday.

1. Monday: branch cut, `release/x.y` created, QA regression starts.
2. Tuesday: submit to App Store review and Play Console internal track.
3. Wednesday: phased rollout starts at 1%, then 10% after 24 h, 50% after 48 h,
   100% after 72 h if the crash-free rate stays above 99.5%.

A hotfix skips the train but still goes through phased rollout.

docs.title: Push notifications
docs.body:
# Push notifications

Pushes go through our notifier service, which fans out to APNs and FCM. Device
tokens are registered on login and deleted on logout.

- Marketing pushes need explicit opt-in and respect quiet hours (22:00-08:00
  local time).
- Transactional pushes (payment received, order shipped) are always sent.
- Invalid tokens reported by APNs/FCM are pruned nightly.

docs.title: Offline sync design
docs.body:
---
description: How the mobile apps queue changes offline and reconcile them.
---


# Offline sync design

## Local store

The apps keep a SQLite mirror of the user's records. Every write goes to a local
*outbox* table first and is shown in the UI immediately.

## Sending the outbox

When connectivity returns, the outbox is flushed in order. Each entry carries a
client-generated UUID so the server can deduplicate a resend.

```kotlin
outbox.pending().forEach { change ->
    api.push(change.id, change.payload)   // server dedupes on change.id
    outbox.markSent(change.id)
}
```

## Conflicts

The server keeps a `version` per record. If the client's base version is stale:

- Scalar fields: **last write wins**, by server receive time.
- List fields (tags, attachments): merged as a set union.
- Deletes win over edits.

The user sees a small banner when one of their edits was overwritten.

## Limits

The outbox holds at most 5,000 entries; beyond that the app asks the user to go
online before editing more.

docs.title: Crash reporting triage
docs.body:
Crashes are grouped by the crash service. The on-call mobile engineer triages
new groups daily: anything above 0.1% of sessions becomes a P1 ticket, a new
crash in the latest release blocks the rollout from widening.

docs.title: Minimum OS versions
docs.body:
The apps support iOS 16+ and Android 9 (API 28)+. We drop an OS version once it
falls below 2% of active devices, announced one release ahead in the app.

docs.title: Deep links
docs.body:
# Deep links

Universal links (iOS) and App Links (Android) use the `app.harbor.example`
domain. The route table lives in `mobile/shared/routes.json` so both apps and
the web fallback agree. Unknown paths open the home screen; they never crash.

docs.title: Release process
docs.body:
---
description: How backend and web changes get from main to production.
---


# Release process

## Cadence

Backend services and the web app deploy on a **train**: Tuesday and Thursday at
10:00 CET. Anything merged to `main` by 09:00 is on the train.

No trains on Fridays, on public holidays, or during the December freeze
(15 December to 5 January). Hotfixes are the exception and need the incident
commander's approval.

## Steps

1. The release captain tags `main` (`vYYYY.MM.DD-N`).
2. CI builds images and runs the smoke suite against staging.
3. Canary: 5% of traffic for 20 minutes, watching error rate and p99 latency.
4. Full rollout if the canary stays inside its SLO budget.

```bash
./scripts/release.sh tag
./scripts/release.sh promote --canary 5
./scripts/release.sh promote --all
```

## Rollback

Rollback is one command and takes about three minutes:

```bash
./scripts/release.sh rollback --to previous
```

Roll back first, investigate second. A rollback never needs approval.

## Release captain

The captain rotates weekly with on-call. They own the train, post the changelog
in #releases and decide whether a flaky canary is a blocker.

## Changelog

Every merged pull request carries a one-line changelog entry in its description
under `Changelog:`. The captain's script collects them per train and groups
them by service. Entries are written for support staff, not for engineers:
say what changed for a merchant, not which function moved.

## What goes on a train

- Anything merged to `main` that passed CI.
- Database migrations, but only the *expand* half; the contract half waits for
  a later train (see the migrations guide).
- Feature work behind a flag that is off by default.

What does not go on a train:

- Changes to the gateway's routing table; those ship in a separate change
  window on Wednesday afternoon with the infra team present.
- Terraform changes; they are applied from CI on their own schedule.

## Hotfixes

A hotfix is a single commit cherry-picked onto the last released tag. It runs
the same canary as a train, only shorter (10 minutes). The incident commander
approves it in the incident channel; the approval message is linked from the
tag. After the hotfix, the same fix must land on `main` before the next train
so it is not lost.

## Metrics we watch

The canary gate compares the canary pods with the stable pods on:

| Signal | Threshold |
|--------|-----------|
| 5xx rate | no more than 0.5 percentage points above stable |
| p99 latency | no more than 20% above stable |
| saturation | CPU and memory under 80% |

If any threshold is breached for three consecutive minutes the script stops and
pings the captain. The captain can override with `--force`, which is logged and
reviewed at the weekly ops review.

docs.title: Incident response runbook
docs.body:
---
description: Severity levels, paging and the postmortem rule.
---


# Incident response runbook

## Severity

| Level | Definition | Response |
|-------|------------|----------|
| SEV1 | Checkout or login down for most users, or data loss | page immediately, all hands |
| SEV2 | Major feature degraded, workaround exists | page on-call, 30 min |
| SEV3 | Minor bug with customer impact | next business day |

## First fifteen minutes

1. Acknowledge the page in PagerTree.
2. Open an incident channel: `/incident open sev2 "short title"`.
3. Name an incident commander (IC). The IC coordinates; they do not debug.
4. Post a status update every 30 minutes, even if nothing changed.
5. If a deploy went out in the last two hours, roll it back before anything else.

## Communication

The IC owns the status page. Customer-facing wording is reviewed by support
before it goes out for SEV1.

## After the incident

A blameless postmortem is written within **five business days** for every SEV1
and SEV2, using the postmortem template. Action items become tickets with an
owner and a due date; they are reviewed at the weekly ops review.

## Roles

- **Incident commander**: owns the timeline, decides on rollbacks, assigns work.
- **Scribe**: keeps the timeline in the channel with UTC timestamps.
- **Subject expert**: whoever knows the failing system best; may change during
  the incident.
- **Communications lead** (SEV1 only): writes status page updates and talks to
  support and account managers.

## Useful commands

```bash
/incident open sev1 "checkout returns 500"
/incident role ic @name
/incident status "mitigated: rolled back train 2026.08.14-2"
/incident close
```

## Escalation

If the on-call primary cannot make progress within 30 minutes on a SEV1, page
the engineering manager on duty. For anything involving personal data, also
page the security lead: a possible data breach has a 72-hour notification
clock, and the legal team needs to know early.

## Closing

An incident is closed when customer impact has ended and the IC has confirmed
that no mitigation is holding things together temporarily. Temporary
mitigations (a disabled feature, a manual scaling change) are listed in the
closing message with a ticket each.

docs.title: On-call rotation
docs.body:
# On-call rotation

One primary and one secondary per week. Handover is Monday 10:00 in the ops
channel, with a written summary of open alerts and ongoing incidents.

- Primary acknowledges pages within 5 minutes, day or night.
- Secondary takes over if the primary does not acknowledge within 10 minutes.
- On-call is compensated with a fixed weekly allowance plus time off in lieu for
  night pages.
- Swaps are fine; update the schedule yourself and tell the other person.

docs.title: Kubernetes cluster layout
docs.body:
# Kubernetes cluster layout

Two clusters per region: `prod-eu-1` and `staging-eu-1`. Namespaces map to
teams (`api`, `web`, `data`). Each service gets requests and limits; limits on
memory are mandatory, limits on CPU are not set (we rely on requests for
scheduling). Ingress is handled by the shared gateway, never per service.

docs.title: Secrets management
docs.body:
# Secrets management

Secrets live in Vault under `secret/<env>/<service>`. Services read them at
start-up through the Vault agent sidecar; nothing is baked into images or
committed to git.

Database credentials are dynamic and expire after 24 hours. Static API keys for
third parties are rotated every 90 days; the rotation calendar is in the infra
wiki. A leaked secret is a SEV2: rotate first, then investigate.

docs.title: Backup and restore
docs.body:
# Backup and restore

Postgres takes continuous WAL archiving plus a nightly base snapshot. Snapshots
are kept for **35 days** in a separate account with object lock.

We run a restore drill every quarter: restore last night's snapshot into a
scratch cluster, replay WAL to a chosen point, and verify row counts against
production. The last drill took 47 minutes end to end.

docs.title: Terraform conventions
docs.body:
Infrastructure is in `infra/terraform`, one state per environment. Modules are
pinned by git tag. `terraform plan` output is posted on the pull request by CI
and a human must approve before `apply`. Never run `apply` from a laptop.

docs.title: CI runners
docs.body:
CI runs on self-hosted runners in the staging cluster, autoscaled from 2 to 40.
Jobs are capped at 30 minutes. Cache keys include the lockfile hash, so a
dependency bump always starts cold.

docs.title: TLS certificate renewal
docs.body:
Public certificates come from the ACME issuer in cert-manager and renew 30 days
before expiry. An alert fires at 14 days left. Internal mTLS certificates are
issued by the mesh and last 24 hours.

docs.title: Cloud cost dashboard
docs.body:
The monthly spend dashboard breaks cost down per team namespace and per
managed service. Any week-on-week jump above 15% posts to the ops channel. The
biggest line items are the database instances and cross-region egress.

docs.title: Warehouse schema conventions
docs.body:
# Warehouse schema conventions

- Raw tables land in `raw_<source>` unchanged.
- Cleaned models live in `staging_*`, business models in `mart_*`.
- Snake_case columns; timestamps in UTC and suffixed `_at`; booleans prefixed
  `is_` or `has_`.
- Every model has a primary key test and a not-null test on it.

docs.title: Nightly ETL jobs
docs.body:
# Nightly ETL jobs

Batch loads are orchestrated by Conveyor. The nightly DAG starts at 02:00 UTC
and must finish by 06:00 UTC so the morning dashboards are fresh.

If a job fails, Conveyor retries twice, then pages the data on-call. Late data
from a source is not a failure: the job waits up to 90 minutes for the source's
completion marker before it gives up.

docs.title: PII handling policy
docs.body:
---
description: Rules for personal data in the warehouse and in analytics events.
---


# PII handling policy

Personal data (names, email addresses, phone numbers, street addresses, IPs)
never enters the `mart_*` layer in clear text.

- Emails are hashed with a keyed SHA-256 before load.
- Free-text fields are excluded unless a scrubber has run over them.
- Access to `raw_*` requires the `pii-reader` role, granted for 30 days at a time.

Erasure requests (GDPR article 17) are processed within 30 days: the account is
deleted in production and its hash is added to the suppression list so the
warehouse drops it on the next load.

docs.title: Metric definition: active user
docs.body:
An **active user** is an account that performed at least one authenticated
action (not just an app open) in the period. DAU, WAU and MAU use calendar days
in UTC. Internal and test accounts are excluded via `is_internal`.

docs.title: Data retention schedule
docs.body:
Raw event data is kept 13 months, aggregated models indefinitely. Application
logs are kept 30 days, audit logs 7 years. Retention is enforced by lifecycle
rules on the buckets, not by scheduled deletes.

docs.title: Event tracking plan
docs.body:
# Event tracking plan

Analytics events are named `object_action` in past tense: `order_placed`,
`coupon_applied`, `signup_completed`. Every event carries `user_id`,
`session_id`, `platform` and `app_version`. New events are added to
`tracking/plan.yaml` first; the schema check in CI rejects unknown events.

docs.title: Dashboard ownership
docs.body:
Every dashboard in the BI tool has one owning team in its description. Unowned
dashboards are archived after 60 days without views. Metrics shown on the exec
dashboard must come from a `mart_*` model with tests.

docs.title: Onboarding for new engineers
docs.body:
---
description: First-week checklist for people joining engineering.
---


# Onboarding for new engineers

## Day one

- Get your laptop from IT and enrol it in device management.
- Ask your buddy for access to the code host, the chat workspace and Vault.
- Read the glossary and the architecture overview.

## First week

- Run the stack locally (see *Local development setup*).
- Ship a small change through the whole release train by Thursday.
- Shadow the on-call engineer for one day.
- Book 30-minute intros with the leads of api, web, mobile, infra and data.

## First month

- Take your first on-call shift as secondary.
- Pick one runbook and improve it.

Your buddy is your first stop for any question. There are no stupid questions in
the first month, or after it.

docs.title: Code review guidelines
docs.body:
# Code review guidelines

- Reviews within one working day. If you cannot, say so and hand it off.
- Keep pull requests under ~400 changed lines; split otherwise.
- Comment on the code, not the person. Prefix optional remarks with `nit:`.
- The author merges after approval, not the reviewer.
- Two approvals for anything touching auth, payments or data deletion.

docs.title: Commit message style
docs.body:
Commits use Conventional Commits: `type(scope): summary` in the imperative,
under 72 characters, e.g. `fix(auth): refresh grace window`. The body explains
why, not what. Reference the ticket as `#123` in the footer.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.body:
# Glossary

- **Merchant** - a business that sells through our platform.
- **Capture** - settling a previously authorised card payment.
- **Train** - a scheduled deploy slot.
- **IC** - incident commander.
- **Beacon** - the feature-flag service.
- **Conveyor** - the batch orchestrator for the warehouse.
- **Outbox** - the mobile app's queue of unsent local changes.

docs.title: Team rituals
docs.body:
Standup is 09:30, fifteen minutes, async in the channel on Fridays. Planning is
every other Monday. The retrospective is every other Friday at 15:00 and is
facilitated by a different person each time. Demo day is the last Thursday of
the month.

docs.title: Decision log index
docs.body:
# Decision log index

| ID | Decision |
|----|----------|
| D12 | Cursor pagination on every list endpoint |
| D27 | Date-based API versions instead of /v2 paths |
| D33 | Last-write-wins for scalar fields in offline sync |
| D41 | 10-second grace window for refresh-token reuse |
| D44 | Memory limits mandatory, CPU limits unset on Kubernetes |
| D52 | Keyed SHA-256 for emails in the warehouse |

docs.title: Security vulnerability disclosure
docs.body:
External researchers report issues to security@harbor.example. We acknowledge
within two business days and aim to fix critical issues within 7 days, high
within 30. Researchers are credited in the changelog unless they ask otherwise.
We do not run a paid bounty programme.

docs.title: Dependency upgrade policy
docs.body:
Renovate opens dependency pull requests every Monday. Patch and minor bumps
auto-merge if CI is green. Major bumps get a human review and a note on what
changed. Nothing stays more than two majors behind upstream.

docs.title: Testing strategy
docs.body:
# Testing strategy

- Unit tests next to the code; fast, no network.
- Integration tests run against real Postgres and Redis in containers.
- End-to-end tests cover the five money paths only (signup, login, checkout,
  refund, payout); they run on every train, not every commit.
- A flaky test is quarantined within a day and fixed or deleted within a week.

docs.title: Postmortem template
docs.body:
---
description: Template for blameless postmortems after SEV1/SEV2 incidents.
---


# Postmortem: <title>

## Summary
One paragraph: what happened, impact, duration.

## Timeline (UTC)
- hh:mm - detection
- hh:mm - mitigation
- hh:mm - resolution

## Root cause
Explain the chain of causes; avoid naming individuals.

## What went well / what went badly

## Action items
| Action | Owner | Due |
|--------|-------|-----|

docs.title: Hiring interview loop
docs.body:
The engineering loop is four conversations: a pairing exercise on a small real
bug, a system design talk, a values interview, and a chat with the hiring
manager. Interviewers submit written feedback before the debrief and do not
discuss the candidate beforehand.

docs.title: Writing style for docs
docs.body:
Docs are written in plain English, second person, present tense. Lead with the
rule, then the reason. One idea per paragraph. Code, paths and flags go in
backticks. Screenshots go stale; prefer text.

docs.title: Local development setup
docs.body:
# Local development setup

```bash
git clone git@code.harbor.example:platform/monorepo.git
cd monorepo
make bootstrap     # installs toolchains via mise
make dev           # docker compose up: postgres, redis, opensearch, mailhog
```

Seed data: `make seed` creates a demo merchant with 200 orders. The web app runs
on http://localhost:5173 and the API on http://localhost:8080. If ports clash,
copy `.env.example` to `.env` and change them there.

docs.title: Database migrations guide
docs.body:
---
description: How to change the Postgres schema without downtime.
---


# Database migrations guide

We deploy several times a week with no maintenance window, so every schema
change must work with both the old and the new application code running at the
same time.

## Expand, migrate, contract

1. **Expand**: add the new column or table, nullable or with a default.
2. **Migrate**: ship code that writes both, then backfill in batches.
3. **Contract**: in a *later* release, remove the old column.

Never rename or drop a column in the same release that stops using it.

## Writing a migration

Migrations are plain SQL files in `db/migrations/`, numbered by timestamp.

```sql
-- 20260812_add_orders_channel.sql
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN channel text;
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_channel ON orders (channel);
```

## Rules

- Indexes on large tables are created `CONCURRENTLY`.
- Backfills run in batches of 10,000 rows with a pause, from a job, not the
  migration file.
- A migration must finish in under 5 seconds of lock time on production-sized
  data; test it against the anonymised snapshot.
- `NOT NULL` on an existing column: add a `CHECK ... NOT VALID` constraint
  first, validate it, then set `NOT NULL`.

## Reviewing

Migrations need a review from someone on the api team, and the pull request must
say which release will carry the contract step.

## Common recipes

### Renaming a column

```sql
-- release N: expand
ALTER TABLE merchants ADD COLUMN display_name text;
-- release N: code writes both name and display_name, reads name
-- job: backfill display_name from name in batches
-- release N+1: code reads display_name
-- release N+2: contract
ALTER TABLE merchants DROP COLUMN name;
```

### Changing a column type

Add a new column with the new type, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, then
drop the old one. Never `ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE` on a table with more than a
million rows: it rewrites the table under an exclusive lock.

### Adding a foreign key

Add it `NOT VALID`, then `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` in a separate migration. The
validation takes only a share lock and does not block writes.

## When a migration goes wrong

If a migration fails halfway on production, do not re-run it by hand. Roll the
application back if needed, then write a new forward migration that repairs the
state. We do not write down-migrations: they are never tested and usually lose
data.

docs.title: Logging conventions
docs.body:
# Logging conventions

Logs are structured JSON with `level`, `msg`, `service`, `request_id` and
`trace_id`. Use `info` for state changes, `warn` for handled problems, `error`
only when a human should look.

Never log personal data or credentials: no email addresses, tokens, card numbers
or request bodies. The log shipper redacts known patterns, but that is a safety
net, not permission.

docs.title: Distributed tracing
docs.body:
All services emit OpenTelemetry spans to the collector. Sampling is 10% of
normal requests and 100% of requests that error or take over 2 seconds. Use the
`trace_id` from a log line to open the whole request in the tracing UI.

docs.title: Caching strategy
docs.body:
# Caching strategy

Read-heavy endpoints cache in Redis with a TTL, never indefinitely. Default TTL
is 5 minutes; catalog data 1 hour. Writes invalidate by key, not by flushing.
The CDN caches static assets for a year (they are content-hashed) and HTML for
0 seconds.

docs.title: Email deliverability
docs.body:
Transactional email goes through our mail relay with SPF, DKIM and DMARC
(`p=quarantine`) on `harbor.example`. Marketing email uses a separate
subdomain so a complaint spike cannot hurt receipts and password resets. Hard
bounces are suppressed immediately.

docs.title: Architecture overview
docs.body:
# Architecture overview

Clients (web, iOS, Android, partner integrations) talk to one gateway. Behind it
sit the core services: accounts, catalog, orders, billing, notifier and search.
Services own their Postgres databases and publish events to the message bus;
the warehouse consumes those events. There is no shared database between
services.

docs.title: Afspraken overdracht klantenservice
docs.body:
# Afspraken overdracht klantenservice

Tickets die de klantenservice doorzet naar engineering krijgen altijd een
voorbeeld-ordernummer en een tijdstip mee. Zonder die twee gegevens gaat het
ticket terug. Engineering reageert binnen één werkdag met een eerste inschatting,
ook als de oplossing langer duurt. Terugbellen naar de klant doet altijd de
klantenservice, nooit een ontwikkelaar.

docs.title: Werkplekvergoeding
docs.body:
Wie thuiswerkt krijgt eenmalig een vergoeding voor een bureaustoel en een
tweede scherm, tot een maximum van 600 euro. Declareren gaat via het
onkostenportaal met de bon erbij, binnen drie maanden na aankoop.

docs.title: Status page
docs.body: The public status page is status.harbor.example, owned by infra.

docs.title: Design review slot
docs.body: Design reviews happen Wednesdays at 14:00; add your doc to the agenda by Tuesday.
